accepted: Vascular cognitive impairment of dementia severity due to probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy (Boston criteria v2.0), with transient focal neurological episodes from cortical superficial siderosis

differential.key_features: The working diagnosis and the reason for the aspirin, but the episodes are stereotyped, spread over two to three minutes and are purely positive sensory phenomena, and MRI shows no infarct but cortical superficial siderosis over the left central sulcus: the pattern of transient focal neurological episodes
The prior haemorrhage was attributed to hypertension, but blood pressure has been well controlled, all eleven microbleeds are strictly lobar and there is no deep or infratentorial microbleed

The episodes spread over minutes rather than seconds, which is the migrainous-spreading rather than the epileptic pattern; siderosis can cause either, and if they persist or evolve an EEG and an antiseizure trial become reasonable

Medial temporal lobes preserved (MTA 1), recognition memory preserved and recall cue-responsive; an amyloid PET, if obtained, is positive but cannot separate vascular from parenchymal amyloid, so coexisting Alzheimer pathology is possible but unproven and does not change management
New stereotyped spreading sensory episodes beginning in the eighth decade in a patient with no migraine history, in the presence of cortical superficial siderosis

key_clinical_evidence: Transient focal neurological episodes are a presenting feature of cortical superficial siderosis and differ from transient ischaemic attacks by being stereotyped, recurrent, positive rather than negative in phenomenology, and spreading over minutes

The distribution rule decides the mechanism: strictly lobar microbleeds with siderosis and a lobar haemorrhage meet Boston v2.0 for probable amyloid angiopathy, whereas any deep haemorrhagic lesion would exclude probable CAA and point to hypertensive or mixed arteriopathy
Misdiagnosing these episodes as transient ischaemic attacks leads to an antithrombotic that increases the risk of the haemorrhage the patient is already prone to

Boston v2.0 adds two white matter features (severe centrum semiovale perivascular spaces, multispot white matter hyperintensity) for patients with a single lobar haemorrhagic lesion; here the haemorrhagic lesions alone meet the criteria
Amyloid PET cannot separate vascular from parenchymal amyloid, so a positive scan does not establish coexisting Alzheimer disease and does not change management here

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Ludovico Sarti is a 76-year-old retired headmaster referred with recurrent stereotyped episodes and cognitive decline. The episodes have occurred about ten times in the past year, are identical each time, and consist of tingling that begins in the right thumb and spreads over two to three minutes up the arm and onto the face before resolving completely. There is no jerking, no loss of awareness and no headache. They were diagnosed as transient ischaemic attacks and he was started on aspirin; they have continued unchanged, and if anything have become more frequent since. Separately, his wife reports two years of cognitive decline: he is slower, forgets conversations unless reminded of the context, has stopped managing the household accounts, and has lost the thread of the reading group he chaired. Four years ago he had a small right lobar intracerebral haemorrhage which was managed conservatively and from which he recovered well; it was attributed to hypertension, although his blood pressure has been well controlled throughout. His mother died of an intracerebral haemorrhage at 82. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuation and no dream enactment.
